report.title: A Brief History of the Python Programming Language
report.summary: Python was conceived in the late 1980s by Guido van Rossum at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC programming language [E8][E9]. Implementation started in December 1989 with the goals of supporting exception handling and interfacing with the Amoeba operating system [E8][E9]. The language was named after the British television show *Monty Python's Flying Circus* [E8][E9].

sections.heading: Early Releases and Major Versions
sections.content:
Van Rossum released Python version 0.9.0 in 1991, followed by version 0.9.1 published to alt.sources in February 1991 [E7][E8]. Early editions already featured classes with inheritance, exception handling, functions, and core datatypes like lists, dictionaries, and strings [E7].

Python 2.0 launched on October 16, 2000, introducing significant additions such as list comprehensions, a cycle-detecting garbage collector, and Unicode support alongside a more transparent development process [E8][E9]. Subsequently, Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, as a major revision that was not completely backward-compatible with earlier versions [E9][E11].

sections.heading: Governance and Modern Development
sections.content: For decades, Van Rossum guided the project as Python's "Benevolent Dictator for Life" (BDFL) until announcing his permanent departure from the role on July 12, 2018 [E8][E9]. In January 2019, active core developers elected a five-member Steering Council to lead the project [E8]. Python operates on an annual release cycle and a five-year support policy [E11], continually evolving to incorporate features like optional static typing and new built-in types [E11][E10].

### Origins and Creation
- Python was conceived in the late 1980s by Guido van Rossum at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC programming language [E8][E9].
- Implementation began in December 1989 [E8][E9]. It was designed to support exception handling and interfacing with the Amoeba operating system [E8][E9], and was named after the BBC TV show *Monty Python's Flying Circus* [E9].

### Early Releases and Development
- Guido van Rossum first released Python version 0.9.0 in 1991, followed by version 0.9.1 published to alt.sources in February 1991 [E7][E8].
- Early features included classes with inheritance, exception handling, functions, and core datatypes like lists, dictionaries, and strings, alongside a module and exception model inspired by Modula-3 [E7].
- Python 2.0 was released on October 16, 2000, introducing list comprehensions, a cycle-detecting garbage collector, Unicode support, and a more transparent community-backed development process [E9].
- Python 3.0 was released in 2008 as a major revision that was not completely backward-compatible with earlier versions [E11].

### Leadership
- Guido van Rossum led the project as Python's "Benevolent Dictator for Life" (BDFL) until July 12, 2018 [E8][E9].
- In January 2019, active core developers elected a five-member Steering Council to lead the project [E8].

# A Brief History of the Python Programming Language

Python was conceived in the late 1980s by Guido van Rossum at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC programming language [E8][E9]. Implementation started in December 1989 with the goals of supporting exception handling and interfacing with the Amoeba operating system [E8][E9]. The language was named after the British television show *Monty Python's Flying Circus* [E8][E9].

## Early Releases and Major Versions

Van Rossum released Python version 0.9.0 in 1991, followed by version 0.9.1 published to alt.sources in February 1991 [E7][E8]. Early editions already featured classes with inheritance, exception handling, functions, and core datatypes like lists, dictionaries, and strings [E7]. 

Python 2.0 launched on October 16, 2000, introducing significant additions such as list comprehensions, a cycle-detecting garbage collector, and Unicode support alongside a more transparent development process [E8][E9]. Subsequently, Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, as a major revision that was not completely backward-compatible with earlier versions [E9][E11].

## Governance and Modern Development

For decades, Van Rossum guided the project as Python's "Benevolent Dictator for Life" (BDFL) until announcing his permanent departure from the role on July 12, 2018 [E8][E9]. In January 2019, active core developers elected a five-member Steering Council to lead the project [E8]. Python operates on an annual release cycle and a five-year support policy [E11], continually evolving to incorporate features like optional static typing and new built-in types [E11][E10].

# A Brief History of the Python Programming Language

Python was conceived in the late 1980s by Guido van Rossum at Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI) in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC programming language [E8][E9]. Implementation started in December 1989 with the goals of supporting exception handling and interfacing with the Amoeba operating system [E8][E9]. The language was named after the British television show *Monty Python's Flying Circus* [E8][E9].

## Early Releases and Major Versions

Van Rossum released Python version 0.9.0 in 1991, followed by version 0.9.1 published to alt.sources in February 1991 [E7][E8]. Early editions already featured classes with inheritance, exception handling, functions, and core datatypes like lists, dictionaries, and strings [E7]. 

Python 2.0 launched on October 16, 2000, introducing significant additions such as list comprehensions, a cycle-detecting garbage collector, and Unicode support alongside a more transparent development process [E8][E9]. Subsequently, Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, as a major revision that was not completely backward-compatible with earlier versions [E9][E11].

## Governance and Modern Development

For decades, Van Rossum guided the project as Python's "Benevolent Dictator for Life" (BDFL) until announcing his permanent departure from the role on July 12, 2018 [E8][E9]. In January 2019, active core developers elected a five-member Steering Council to lead the project [E8]. Python operates on an annual release cycle and a five-year support policy [E11], continually evolving to incorporate features like optional static typing and new built-in types [E11][E10].
